title: Mansa Musa, the Richest Man in History
author: Léxi
desc: Le roi du Mali qui fit tomber le prix de l'or en Égypte pendant son voyage à La Mecque.

p: In the year 1312, a new king came to the throne of the Mali Empire. His name was Musa Keita. People called him *Mansa* Musa, which means "King of Kings".
The Mali Empire was enormous. It went from the Atlantic Ocean to the middle of the Sahara desert. It was bigger than many countries of Europe together.
And it was rich. Very rich. Mali had some of the biggest gold mines in the world. At that time, about half of the gold in the Mediterranean world came from West Africa.
Today, many historians say that Mansa Musa was the richest person in all of human history. Richer than any king, any businessman, any billionaire.
Mansa Musa was a Muslim. In 1324, he decided to go on pilgrimage to Mecca, in Arabia. The journey was more than six thousand kilometres.
But he didn't travel like a normal person. He travelled with a caravan of about sixty thousand people. There were soldiers, servants, doctors, teachers and merchants.
The stories say that hundreds of camels carried gold. Each camel carried about a hundred kilos.
Everywhere he went, Mansa Musa gave gold to the poor. He built mosques. People said that he built a new mosque every Friday.
When the caravan arrived in Cairo, in Egypt, the people could not believe their eyes. Mansa Musa spent so much gold and gave so many gifts that something strange happened.
There was so much gold in the city that its value went down. For about ten years, gold in Cairo was cheaper than before.
An Arab writer, Al-Umari, visited Cairo some years later. He wrote that people still talked about the King of Mali and his generosity.
On a famous map from 1375, the Catalan Atlas, there is a picture of Mansa Musa. He is sitting on a throne, with a crown, holding a big golden ball. The whole world now knew about Mali.
Mansa Musa came home with something more precious than gold: knowledge.
He brought back scholars, poets and an architect called Abu Ishaq es-Saheli. Together, they built the great Djinguereber Mosque in Timbuktu. It still stands today, made of earth and wood.

Timbuktu became a great city of learning. Students came from all over Africa and the Arab world. They studied mathematics, astronomy, medicine, law and poetry. There were thousands of books, written by hand.
Some of these manuscripts still exist today. Families in Timbuktu protected them for centuries.
Mansa Musa's lesson is simple: gold is spent and disappears. But knowledge, when you share it, grows forever.
